snapshots.name: Christ
snapshots.body: Jesus Christ, the book's central figure and its constant addressee, spoken to as "Thou" throughout and also named directly, over a hundred times, as Christ, Jesus, and the Son of Man. Much of Books III and IV is written as his own first-person counsel to the reader ("My Son..."), and Book IV's alternating "Voice of Christ" sections give him an explicit speaking part in its staged dialogue with the Disciple.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Disciple
snapshots.body: The book's other named voice: the reader's own persona, addressed by Christ as "My Son" and speaking in turn, given an explicit label -- "The Voice of the Disciple" -- heading alternating sections throughout Book IV's staged dialogue on the Eucharist. In Books I-III the same first-person voice is the ordinary, unnamed-narrator convention of a devotional treatise, and is not labelled.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Holy Ghost
snapshots.body: The Holy Ghost, the third person of the Trinity, invoked several times for the peace, grace, and consolation he brings, and named once by his Greek title, "the Paraclete." original-en's "Holy Ghost" is modern-en's "Holy Spirit" throughout; both phrasings are aliased so the entity binds in both editions.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John the Baptist
snapshots.body: The forerunner of Christ, invoked twice as a model of holiness ("the holiness of holy John the Baptist") and of joyful humility before Christ's presence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Job
snapshots.body: The patriarch of the Book of Job, quoted directly once as "holy Job" on God's visiting and testing him -- distinct from the book's many footnote citations of "Job" as a scriptural source, which are never bound (see module docstring).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Luke
snapshots.body: The evangelist, named once in the running prose as the source of a Gospel saying ("as the Evangelist Luke hath it"), distinct from the book's many footnote citations of the Gospel of Luke, which are never bound.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Moses
snapshots.body: The lawgiver, invoked several times: the children of Israel's plea that he, not God directly, should speak to them; his resort to the tabernacle for counsel; and his building of the ark of the covenant to house the tables of the law.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Samuel
snapshots.body: The prophet, invoked once as a model of humble receptivity to God's voice ("rather with Samuel the prophet, I beseech Thee").
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Solomon
snapshots.body: The king of Israel, invoked once for the seven years he spent building his temple, as a point of comparison for the reader's own preparation to receive the Eucharist.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Noah
snapshots.body: The patriarch, invoked once for the hundred years he spent building the ark, as the same point of comparison.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Joshua
snapshots.body: The leader of Israel, invoked once for having been deceived by the Gibeonites after failing to ask counsel of God first -- a warning against trusting outward appearances.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: David
snapshots.body: The king and psalmist, invoked once for dancing before the Ark of God and composing the Psalms, as an example of wholehearted devotion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Paul
snapshots.body: The apostle, invoked four times: for teaching that God makes a way to escape temptation, that true approval comes from God alone, for having been caught up to the third heaven yet still called to suffer, and for striving to please all men for the sake of their salvation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Peter
snapshots.body: The apostle, invoked once ("the blessed Apostle Peter beseecheth") for teaching that Christ's faithful should live as strangers and pilgrims in the world.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mary Magdalene
snapshots.body: Named once in full as rising quickly from her grief when Martha told her Jesus had come and called for her, and again, unnamed beyond the bare "Mary," as one of the sisters of Bethany whom the crowds came to see alongside the raised Lazarus -- the same traditional identification of Mary of Bethany with Mary Magdalene this genre of devotional writing generally assumes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Virgin Mary
snapshots.body: The mother of Christ, named in full once, as the model of faith and purity with which the Disciple longs to receive the Eucharist, as she once received the angel's tidings of the Incarnation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Martha
snapshots.body: Sister of Mary and Lazarus at Bethany, who tells Mary that Jesus has come and calls for her, and who receives the crowd that comes to see the raised Lazarus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lazarus
snapshots.body: The brother of Martha and Mary at Bethany, raised from the dead by Jesus; the crowds who came to Bethany, the text notes, came not for Jesus's sake but to see him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zacchaeus
snapshots.body: The tax collector who welcomed Jesus into his house, invoked as a model for the Disciple's own desire to receive Christ worthily in Holy Communion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Abraham
snapshots.body: The patriarch, invoked once as the Disciple hopes to be "numbered among the children of Abraham" through receiving Communion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Satan
snapshots.body: The devil, named once as the source of the evil suggestions that trouble those preparing for Holy Communion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adam
snapshots.body: The first man, named once as the source, through his Fall, of the corruption of human nature inherited by all his descendants.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eve
snapshots.body: The first woman, named once via the phrase "the exiled sons of Eve," for humanity's shared exile and mourning in this life.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: St. Francis
snapshots.body: Francis of Assisi, quoted once for his teaching on humility: "What each one is in Thine eyes, so much he is, and no more."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Laurence
snapshots.body: The early Christian martyr, cited once for overcoming his love of the world and of his own priestly master, Sixtus, for the love of Christ.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sixtus
snapshots.body: Pope Sixtus II, named once as the "chief priest" and beloved master whom Laurence calmly let be taken from him for the love of God.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: St. Agatha
snapshots.body: The early Christian martyr, named once in an editorial footnote identifying the source of a quoted line as her own words, rather than a scriptural citation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.
